newsitem.title: ANGOLA: U.N. chief speaks to crowd, calls for landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief speaks to crowd, calls for landmine ban.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan spoke to a cheering crowd during a driving rainstorm on Sunday, but the bad weather forced the cancellation of a scheduled meeting with UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi.
"It saddens me to see the destruction here," said Annan, speaking in Kuito's town square, surrounded by bombed-out and bullet-riddled municipal buildings.

"I want to assure the Angolan people that the international community and the United Nations in particular will continue to assist the Angolan people in their quest for peace and reconciliation," he said.
Annan visited the central highlands city, site of vicious fighting between government and UNITA troops in 1993 and 1994, during a four-day trip to Angola.
U.N. officials said the rains were too heavy for the aircraft carrying Annan to land safely in nearby Bailundo, where Savimbi has his headquarters.
The talks have apparently been rescheduled for Monday morning in Bailundo, according to U.N. sources.

The former UNITA rebel movement and the government signed a peace accord in 1994. The 2-1/2 years of peace since then is the longest peace the country has known since it plunged into civil war on independence from Portugal in 1975.
Annan's visit comes at a time when Angola's long peace process shows signs of progress.

The U.N. peacekeeping mission here, the largest in the world, is meant to oversee the implementation of the accord. The establishment of a unity government -- signalling a formal end of hostilities between the two sides -- could come as early as the end of the month.
On Friday UNITA agreed to send its remaining deputies to take up their seats in the National Assembly and members of the national unity government to Luanda.
But as of nightfall on Sunday, the planeload of UNITA deputies had failed to appear.

Annan also used the occasion at Kuito to call for a ban on the production and use of landmines, highlighted in January by Britain's Princess Diana, who paid a high profile visit to mine victims in Angola to campaign for a global ban on the weapons.

"I have witnessed the destruction of people in Kuito," Annan said. "It has been particularly sad to see so many landmine victims. What I have seen reinforces my determination to do what I can to ban the production and use of landmines."
